vignette:
Malik, a 30-year-old African American curriculum designer who lived alone and kept to himself since the breakup, came to treatment after nearly a year of feeling as if his body and mind no longer belonged to the same life. The violence began in the apartment he had shared with his former boyfriend, during one night that started with drinking and escalated into a brutal assault. Malik remembered the sharp, sour smell of alcohol on his partner's breath before the first shove, the sting of being thrown against the kitchen counter, and a burnt smell from a pan left too long on the stove while he tried to protect himself. He had also been hearing the casual comments of family members about "who he was with" and "when he would settle down," and after the assault those remarks felt charged with danger, as if any mention of family could expose him again to shame, disbelief, or blame. The more those everyday cues appeared, the more Malik was pulled back into the event: a whiff of alcohol from a colleague at work, or burnt food drifting from the break room microwave, could make him suddenly feel the same terror he felt that night. At those moments, the memory did not come as a neutral recollection but as a bodily return; he would feel physical pain in the same places he had been struck, and the fear would be so immediate that he often had to stop what he was doing and steady himself. 

As the months passed, Malik found that remembering the assault made everything around him feel dangerous and contaminated. When the memory surged back, he was flooded with the same terror and a harsh conviction that what had happened was deeply unfair and that nothing had been done about it. He also felt dirty in a way he could not fully explain, as though the abuse had left a stain on him that showering, changing clothes, or trying to "move on" could not wash away. The recollection of the event and the bodily pain it brought with it seemed to confirm his sense that the person he had become was unrecognisable to him. He had once seen himself as composed, competent, and generous, someone who could build curricula for other people's children with patience and care; now he felt reduced, altered, and ashamed, as if the assault had rewritten him. Each time the memory returned through the scent of alcohol or burnt food, it deepened that belief, and each time he encountered a family-related comment, the old terror and hurt made him think again that the world had allowed something profoundly unjust to happen and had left him to carry the damage alone. 

In the practical rhythm of his days, these links kept tightening. At work, Malik began avoiding the staff lounge because it was where people lingered with drinks after meetings, and he found himself scanning the room before entering any shared space, alert for the smell of alcohol or anything burnt from the toaster oven. He had become especially tense during curriculum presentations that included family narratives or discussion prompts, because even a passing remark about parents, siblings, or home life could send him back into the same fearful state. The triggers did not merely remind him of the assault; they seemed to summon the memory in full, and the memory, in turn, made him more watchful for those same cues. He started taking longer routes through the office to avoid the kitchenette, declined invitations to after-work gatherings, and made excuses when relatives suggested he come to family dinners. The isolation fit his belief that he was no longer recognisable and that the damage in him would show if he let people too close. It also fed the sense that what had happened was not only unfair but unresolved, because nothing in his daily life felt repaired or safe enough to disprove it. 

By the time he sought help, Malik described feeling worn down by the constant anticipation of the next reminder. He was afraid that a smell on the train, a comment from a cousin, or the drift of burnt toast at work would again bring back the terror, the pain, and the certainty that he had been permanently changed. What he hoped for was less about forgetting than about no longer feeling contaminated by what was done to him, and about finding a way to recognize himself again.
